newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN assembly asked to end "business as usual".
newsitem.headline: UN assembly asked to end "business as usual".

text.p: The General Assembly opened its 51st annual session on Tuesday with a call by its newly elected president for an end to "business as usual" and for action to eradicate poverty and social injustice.
"The occasions of delays and long lunches which lead to more delays, at enormous cost, are over," said Razali Ismail, Malaysia's veteran U.N. envoy who was elected by acclamation.
"I hope that the syndrome of 'business as usual' will be discarded ... Clearly what we produce from our deliberations must matter, must make a difference."

Wearing national dress, the 57-year-old Razali told representatives of 185 countries: "Maybe U.N. delegates are too distant from the problems they are charged to address, and the camaraderie of diplomatic life has softened the edges of critical judgment."
He said the United Nations "must begin to embed itself in reality and push the critical issues, especially poverty and social injustice to the centre of national and public debate."

Suggesting diplomacy was too important to be left solely to diplomats, he said it was "a moot point whether we should delegate the solution of global problems to international diplomacy alone," since it took months, if not years, to negotiate and implement international agreements.
The session opened under a looming dispute over the choice of a secretary-general.

Despite widespread support for Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the United States has served notice it will use its veto if necessary to block another five-year term for the Egyptian diplomat, who turns 74 on Nov. 14. It says the United Nations needs new leadership to carry out reforms.
Razali, whose country is one of the few publicly opposing Boutros-Ghali's re-election, mainly because of his performance over Bosnia, maintained impartiality on that issue.

He only expressed confidence that the Security Council, which nominates a secretary-general, and the Assembly, which appoints him or her, would "play a constructive role and with wisdom and impartiality, determine a course of action that will protect and enhance the integrity" of the United Nations.
The Assembly session contrasts with last year's 50th jubilee celebrations that brought some 150 world leaders to New York. Probably fewer than 40 heads of state or government are expected this time.
The United Nations, perenially short of cash, is owed some $2.9 billion in unpaid regular and peacekeeping dues, more than half of the total by the United States.
The rainy, overcast day began with the ringing by Boutros-Ghali of a peace bell in the U.N. grounds, marking the organisation's annual Day of Peace.

The Assembly spends the rest of the week organising its agenda and completing other chores before embarking next Monday on a three-week general debate with the participation of scores of foreign ministers and other dignitaries.

Hanging over the session is the latest crisis sparked by Baghdad's decision late last month to send its troops into the Kurdish-populated north of Iraq for the first time since the end of the 1991 Gulf War, prompting retaliatory U.S. cruise missile strikes.
Though not an issue for the Assembly -- and one on which the Security Council itself is divided -- the continuing crisis is bound to figure in many ministers' speeches and meetings.
Clinton is due to address the Assembly next Tuesday and Boutros-Ghali, whom he had vowed to replace, is almost certain to be sitting behind him on the podium.

Speaking soon afterward will be Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, followed by Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
The foreign ministers of Germany, China and France are all scheduled address the Assembly next Wednesday.
